One idea runs through the whole piece: Renaissance codex drawings, Vitruvian geometry and perspective construction lines laid over painterly scenes, so the main title visual fits the subject of the show
Many layers in every frame: vellum and stain textures, ink spatter, mirror-script handwriting, sepia washes and violet glazes
Each frame has a different composition: wide architecture, a tight hand and quill, a horizon split with a ghosted Mona Lisa, a low-angle heroic portrait, a figure cut into a schematic
The credit typography is plain small-caps serif, but its placement follows the negative space of each image, and its period tone suits the piece
The motion between shots can be read from the frames: construction lines radiate across the image and illustration turns into mechanism, which points to planned transitions
gaps: The credit type is safe and fairly generic in its weight and tracking. It could be drawn into the codex lines, or pick up their hand and mirror-script quality
The violet-and-sepia grade is applied evenly to every shot. A tighter palette arc across the sequence would give it more of a shape
Some of the illustrated figures, like the portrait and the crossbow man, are close to digital-painting convention. More graphic restraint would make them more distinctive

gaps: The idea is the well-worn luxury-holiday 'magic object flies through the city' formula. It needs a twist the viewer has not seen before

No typographic or graphic layer exists to give the film a signature. A titled or graphic end beat with real typographic character would make it memorable

defects: Dial printing is broken at 100%: 'ATELIER VAUCLAIR' and 'CALIBRE 9' have missing and fragmented strokes, with letters broken or merged. It reads like a failed text-on-curve or displacement render, and on a watch that is the product.
Heavy moiré and aliasing on the wavy guilloché and the sunburst centre. The fine line pattern beats against the pixel grid and will shimmer in motion.
The end card is undercut: the window-shadow bars pass over 'Monday.', and the 'Calibre 9 · 150 pieces' line is low-contrast, small and partly lost in the shadow.
Around 8–9 s the scene goes nearly static (1.7 change/s) right before the end card. That is dead air, not a held beat.
Hand motion blur is a smeared ghost trail rather than true shutter blur. It reads as a CG post effect.
Opening frame: the crown is cropped awkwardly, with a large empty black area and no clear compositional anchor.
The music sections change in rigid 2.4 s blocks (about 2.4 / 4.8 / 7.3 / 9.7 s). This suggests a grid-built edit rather than one shaped to the action.
gaps: Motion is almost entirely slow camera drift and light sweeps over a static hero object, with no mechanical choreography. Nothing in the watch acts: no crown pull, no hands snapping to a time, no movement detail. Energy has no real peak at 60–80%; the busiest second is followed by a dead hold instead of a build and release.

Finish falls short of luxury-watch standards. Dial type is illegible or broken, the guilloché aliases, and there is no lens character. Missing are depth-of-field falloff and real highlight behaviour on polished steel (bloom, anisotropic streaks). The premium promise falls apart at 1:1.

The sound is a tick-click layer plus a fairly static tonal pad and keys in block sections, with no Foley for metal, glass or the mechanism. The low end is the same throughout, and nothing is held back to make room for the 'Monday.' payoff. The ticks fit the subject, but they are a library loop, not designed sound.
